c6dc9ed66e2d.title: Architecture (ArchiMate)
c6dc9ed66e2d.content: . The journeys and systems of this demonstrator, drawn as an ArchiMate overlay on the DPI-H Reference Architecture’s own ArchiMate model (smart-ra, version 0.3.0-draft.1). The RA’s elements are unchanged and keep their ids, so each RA box here is the element smart-ra publishes. The overlay adds: . | the journeys J1 to J4.1 (the use cases) as business processes, one per BPMN process; | the people who take part, as business roles assigned to the journeys whose BPMN has their lane; | each of those roles associated with the RA stakeholder it belongs to: the caregiver with Citizens / Care recipients, the clinicians and the community health worker with Health Workers (a role and a stakeholder are different element types, so ArchiMate allows an association, not a specialization); | the Taifafeki and Onesan systems, serving the journeys they take part in, each holding its parts, each part named by what it does (Patient record, Smart forms (SDC), Health workforce registry (CHWs, nurses)); the family’s shared phone is a technology device that realizes the wallet app on it, not software; | for each country, its own instance of every RA building block its parts play, such as Provider Systems (Taifafeki) and Provider Systems (Onesa): Taifafeki and Onesa are different jurisdictions, so a Taifafeki part realizes Taifafeki’s instance, as the RA draws a concrete system realizing the component it plays (its Table 3.3), and that instance is a specialization of the RA’s block; | where the two countries meet, as flow and triggering relationships between their parts, read from the BPMN: the paper DVC that J1 prints and the family carries to J2 and J3; in J4.1, the VHL QR the family’s phone shows the Taifafeki clinic, the clinic’s signed ITI-YY5 manifest request to the Onesan gateway, and the manifest it returns, the access logged in Onesa; | what they share, and nothing else, between them: WHO GDHCN and the WHO SMART Trust specifications it realizes; | the RA’s own building blocks, generic and no country’s, in a band of their own below both countries in each journey’s view; | each journey’s realization of the RA capabilities it exercises. | . Every line is routed orthogonally through the gaps between boxes and never through a box, and ends on a side of its box clear of the box’s type label. Every element names its concept in the glossary (skosConcept), drawn from the same sources as the model, and every role and system names the FHIR ActorDefinition it realizes (fhir-actor). Every box in a drawing links to its element’s page. All views and elements. Systems on the Integrated View . Two columns: Taifafeki on the left, Onesa on the right. In each, the country’s systems stack top to bottom in the order of the first journey they serve, each holding its parts, and each part says inside its own box which DPI-H RA building block it plays, as a tag such as «Provider Systems». A system’s parts that meet the other country, or GDHCN, sit on the side facing the middle, and each Taifafeki system stands level with the first Onesan system it meets, so the dashed lines where the countries meet run across. Between the columns, only what both share: WHO GDHCN and the SMART Trust specifications. The countries’ instances of the RA blocks, the parts’ realizations of them, and the RA’s own blocks are in the model and drawn in each journey’s view, which keeps this one narrow and its lines few. Journeys (use cases) . One view per journey . | Journey | View | . | J1 Issue the birth-dose DVCs | J1 on the DPI-H RA | . | J2 Discover and refer the infant | J2 on the DPI-H RA | . | J3 Verify, import and schedule | J3 on the DPI-H RA | . | J4.0 Issue the family’s VHLs | J4.0 on the DPI-H RA | . | J4.1 Read records at the point of care | J4.1 on the DPI-H RA | . How it is made . The model is generated, not drawn: python3 -I tools/archimate/build.py fetches smart-ra’s model and its add_views.py at the commit in tools/archimate/smart-ra.lock.json (sha256 checked), applies tools/archimate/overlay.py, lays the overlay’s views out again with room between the boxes and routes every line orthogonally as Archi bendpoints (tools/archimate/layout.py), and writes archimate/0.1.0/smart-trust-demo.archimate. The journeys and their people are read from processes/content/ and scenarios/roles.json, and where the countries meet from the BPMN’s sequence flows; the systems are the system actors of scenarios/actors/, and their parts each actor’s meta.parts (first drawn as VaxLink’s architecture view). tools/ig-gen/ig_gen.py writes the glossary from the same sources. CI fails if the committed model is not what the build makes. The drawings are cat-harness’s archimate subgraph’s: no Archi, no Java. Edit this page on GitHub .

18312dedd641.title: Business Processes
18312dedd641.content: . One business process per journey. Each lane is a role on the personas page; each task names the skill that performs it. The BPMN source of each process is in processes/content/, copied into the guide as input/business-processes/. Select a step’s title to open it, or open a process in the process viewer, which lists each task and the skill that performs it. | Process | Lanes | BPMN | . | J1 Issue the newborn’s birth-dose DVCs in Country A | Caregiver, Birth clinic vaccinator, Birth clinic issuing system, Issuer signing key | j1-birth-dose-dvc.bpmn | . | J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B | Caregiver, Community health worker, CHW app | j2-chw-discovery-referral.bpmn | . | J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic | Caregiver, Home clinic provider, Home clinic EHR | j3-clinic-verification-schedule.bpmn | . | J4.0 Issue the family’s records to one phone as VHLs | Caregiver, National health portal, Issuer signing key, Family phone | j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.bpmn | . | J4.1 Read a family member’s records at the point of care abroad | Caregiver, Family phone, Point-of-care provider, Point-of-care receiver, National health portal | j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.bpmn | . J1 Issue the newborn’s birth-dose DVCs in Country A . Process id Process_J1BirthDoseDvc. Open in the process viewer. J1, Cross-border birth and initial vaccination. In Country A (XXR, the birth country) the provincial hospital gives a newborn who is not its own country’s national the Hep B and BCG birth doses and issues one signed DVC per dose (DVCMinPreQual at subclaim -6) as a paper QR, with no national identity number needed (the WHO guide’s QR Code Generation section 12 example is such a pair). The hospital system is the Issuer (SMART Trust) and the HCERT side of the VHL Sharer; the private key stays with the key holder (two-phase signing, STT-ISS-004, STT-COS-006). XXR’s DSC, under its CSCA, being on the GDHCN trust list is a PRECONDITION of issuing, declared below, not a step. The caregiver is the Holder (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) and VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL). Task checklist: j1-birth-dose-dvc.checklist.md. J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B . Process id Process_J2ChwDiscovery. Open in the process viewer. J2, Return home, CHW discovery and referral. Back in Country B (home, XXK), where the family resides, the community health worker finds an infant born abroad who is missing from the household roster on a home visit. Offline, the CHW app adds the infant to the household (a FHIR Group, through a structured data capture form), reads the foreign DVCs without verifying them (read-unverified, STT-VER-011: the triage read stops before the trust lookup and marks every field unverified), saves the doses as reported by the family, not verified (Immunization.primarySource false), and refers the infant to the clinic for verification. Everything is queued on the phone and syncs when it next has a signal. The CHW app is a Receiver (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) that deliberately stops before trust; the caregiver provides the VDHC as Holder (smart-trust-phw requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver). Task checklist: j2-chw-discovery-referral.checklist.md. J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic . Process id Process_J3ClinicVerification. Open in the process viewer. J3, Clinic verification and schedule generation, in Country B. The clinic EHR (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, VHL Receiver side in IHE ITI VHL) holds a copy of the GDHCN trust list, which the trust anchor (Trust Network Anchor; IHE Trust Anchor) distributes and Country B, a Trust Network Participant, retrieves (smart-trust-phw retrieve-pki-material). Loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the clinic may be offline throughout, so the list it verifies against is the one it last refreshed, about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office. It verifies each foreign DVC in the STT-VER-001 order against XXR’s DSC DID document, imports the verified doses with provenance, adds the national schedule code beside each foreign vaccine code (ConceptMap; the nurse decides any product with no mapping) and evaluates the national schedule, which finds the 6-week doses due and books them. Task checklist: j3-clinic-verification-schedule.checklist.md. J4.0 Issue the family’s records to one phone as VHLs . Process id Process_J40FamilyVhl. Open in the process viewer. J4.0, Outbound family travel, “One Family, One Phone”. Before travelling, the caregiver who holds the family’s one shared phone asks Country B’s national portal for each family member’s records, choosing for each a passcode the family can say aloud and an expiry (for example 14 days); the portal records that choice as the holder’s consent to share (FHIR Consent, IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR). The portal, a VHL Sharer (IHE ITI VHL) and Issuer (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw), issues one passcode-protected Verifiable Health Link per member: the documents (IPS, DVCs) encrypted as JWE (STT-VHL-007) behind an ITI-YY5 manifest, the link in the SMART Health Links payload format at HCERT key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B’s DSC. The shared phone holds the QRs for the caregiver, the VHL Holder. The records themselves stay hosted in Country B: the QR carries only a pointer and a key. Task checklist: j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.checklist.md. J4.1 Read a family member’s records at the point of care abroad . Process id Process_J41VhlFetch. Open in the process viewer. J4.1. Abroad, a child of the family needs care. The caregiver, the VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL; Holder in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver), opens her QR on the family phone and tells the passcode. The hospital system, a VHL Receiver (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw), verifies the HCERT against the GDHCN trust list, requests the manifest by ITI-YY5 with an HTTP Message Signature (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008) and decrypts the documents (STT-VHL-007). Country B’s portal checks the passcode, returns the manifest and logs every request, granted or refused, as an AuditEvent at home (IHE BALP). If the HCERT does not verify, there is no digital verification: the VHL is not followed and the records are treated like paper. As in J3, loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the hospital verifies against its cached copy of the trust list and needs no connection to do so. It refreshes that cache nightly or hourly, where an offline site such as the J3 clinic refreshes about weekly. Task checklist: j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.checklist.md. Edit this page on GitHub .

7fc3330c3e7c.title: Fictional Countries
7fc3330c3e7c.content: . The journeys take place in two fictional countries, so that no real country, ministry or signing key is implied. Each is defined once, in scenarios/countries/, with a code from the ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 user-assigned range (XAA to XZZ), which never names a real country. Other journeys, such as the pilgrimage, reuse the same two countries and codes. | Country | Code | Role | Places | In these journeys | . | Onesa (adjective: Onesan) | XXK | home | Lomaru (capital), Village 04, Tanavu (coastal town) | Country B: the family’s home (J2, J3, J4.0), whose national portal serves their records abroad (J4.1); the pilgrim’s home in the pilgrimage | . | Taifafeki (adjective: Taifafeki) | XXR | visited | Lumara (capital), Kesaro (border province), Nalemi (tent valley), Toreva (plain) | Country A: where the newborn is born (J1) and later seen at the point of care (J4.1); the host of the pilgrimage | . Codes . Both codes are in the SMART Trust value set of GDHCN DEV participants, Participants-DEV, whose code system names XXK “Onesa” and XXR “Taifafeki”. Both are onboarded test participants of the GDHCN DEV network (WorldHealthOrganization/tng-participants-dev): XXR’s document signer key signs the birth-dose DVCs of J1, and XXK plays Onesa’s national portal in J4. Their keys are test keys, not any ministry’s. Reuse . A journey that needs a home country and a visited country takes Onesa and Taifafeki from scenarios/countries/onesa.json and scenarios/countries/taifafeki.json: the name, adjective, code, role and places. The people in a journey are its own, and fictional too. Edit this page on GitHub .

0c671d6cff1d.title: Decision-support Logic
0c671d6cff1d.content: . The decision-support logic is the DAK’s component 6: the decisions the journeys make, as decision tables in the OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN 1.3), as the WHO SMART Guidelines DAK writes them. Each table names the business-process tasks it serves, the requirements it applies, the data elements it reads and the FHIR artifacts that show it in the examples. Each is also a PlanDefinition (type eca-rule) with one action per rule, so it is listed in the artifact index. The sources are processes/content/decisions/*.dmn; this page and the PlanDefinitions are generated from them. The entries use the FEEL subset the harness’s decision-table interpreter accepts: - (any), literals, comparisons and one-of. Every table’s hit policy is FIRST: the rules are tried in order and the first that matches applies, so the order is part of the logic. 8a5edab28263.doc: SMART Trust demonstrator: journeys J1 to J4
8a5edab28263.title: SMART Trust demonstrator: journeys J1 to J4
8a5edab28263.content: . One baby · two countries · one year Somsak is born in Taifafeki and grows up in Onesa. A year later, a Taifafeki doctor sees every vaccine he has ever had, and no record is copied across the border. This guide is that story, told as the journeys J1 to J4, written down as a WHO SMART Guidelines digital adaptation kit (L2) and a FHIR implementation guide (L3). It is built on the SMART Trust HCERT libraries and WHO GDHCN. Walk through the journeys Read the journeys See the FHIR examples Four moments that matter . Each moment is one business process (BPMN), played by fictional people. Each one is linked to the user scenario, the process and the FHIR records it creates. Click a picture to walk through that moment in the journeys walkthrough. 1. Born abroad Birth day · Kesaro, Taifafeki · J1 An Onesan baby gets his first vaccines in Taifafeki. The hospital signs each dose as a Digital Vaccination Certificate, and the family leaves with two paper QR cards. Walk through it · Scenario · Process · Taifafeki profile 2. Found at home 3 weeks later · Village 04, Onesa · J2 A health worker registers him offline and reads the cards. She records them as "reported, not yet verified" and refers him to the clinic. Walk through it · Scenario · Process · Onesan profile 3. Made official 4 weeks later · district health centre, Onesa · J3 A nurse checks the signatures against the GDHCN trust list, offline. She maps the Taifafeki vaccine codes to the Onesan schedule and books the 6-week doses. Walk through it · Scenario · Process · Onesan profile 4. Crossing back 12 months later · Onesa → Taifafeki · J4.0, J4.1 The family shares his whole record with a Taifafeki doctor through a Verifiable Health Link on Dad's phone. Every access is logged back home. Walk through it · Scenario · Process · Onesan profile What is in this guide . |   | What | Where | . | People | Five fictional adults and a baby; the generic personas and system actors who play each process lane | Personas, system actors | . | Journeys | The story moment by moment, with the user scenarios and what each person needs | Journeys J1–J4, user scenarios | . | Workflows | One BPMN process per journey: every lane a role, every task a skill | Business processes | . | Requirements | Where the journeys’ requirements are defined, in smart-trust-tools | Functional requirements | . | Taifafeki profiles | The birth hospital’s patient and dose (the source of each DVC), and the record a Taifafeki clinic keeps when it reads a VHL | Country profiles | . | Onesan profiles | The child and household the CHW registers, reported and verified doses, the referral, DVC verification, and the access log | Country profiles | . | Terminology and logic | Vaccine products, the Onesan schedule codes, the ConceptMap between them, and the infant schedule as a PlanDefinition | Journey examples | . | Examples | Every screen and payload of the journeys walkthrough as a FHIR example, Taifafeki and Onesan | Journey examples | . How trust works here . Taifafeki and Onesa never connect to each other. Both build on WHO GDHCN. Taifafeki publishes the key it signs certificates with, and Onesa caches the trust list, so its clinics can verify a Taifafeki card with no signal. A year later the same trust list lets a Taifafeki clinic verify the Onesan VHL. Data crosses the border in only two ways: as a signed QR card the family carries, or as a link the family chooses to share. The journeys walkthrough’s “How it works” view lays out both countries’ components on the DPI-H reference architecture, with GDHCN as the foundation; the same picture as an ArchiMate overlay on the RA’s own model is on the architecture page. The journeys run the HCERT and VHL libraries of smart-trust-tools against WHO SMART Trust and WHO SMART Trust PHW. The project . The plan, the app-platform proposal and the dependency register. Source: litlfred/smart-trust-demo. Every person and record here is fictional, and every key is a test key. This guide is a demonstrator, not WHO guidance. Edit this page on GitHub .

131f2e7ff2aa.content: . Somsak is born in Taifafeki, grows up in Onesa, and one year later a Taifafeki doctor can see every vaccine he has ever had, without a single record being copied across the border. The story is the one the journeys walkthrough tells, moment by moment, with the people, the technical layer and the policy questions (interactive; its source is web/ in this repository), documented here as a WHO SMART Guidelines L2 DAK and L3 implementation guide. Its FHIR examples are materialized in this guide; the Journey examples page maps each moment and device screen to them. | Country A (birth country) is Taifafeki. Somsak is born at Kesaro Provincial Hospital and gets his birth doses there (J1). The family lives there (J2, J3, J4.0). On the DEV network it is played by a fictional participant, written XXK. | J4.1 takes the family back to Taifafeki, a year later. | . XXR and XXK are DEV test participants, not either country’s production keys, and nothing here implies a real ministry. Every person is fictional. The cast: Khamla SENGMANY (mother), Bounmy SENGMANY (father, holds the family phone), Vilay (community health worker, Village 04), Nurse Chanthason (Lomaru District Health Center) and Dr Anan (Taifafeki clinician, at the birth and a year later). | # | Moment | When | Where | Processes | . | 1 | Born abroad | birth day, 2025-10-28 | Kesaro, Taifafeki | J1 | . | 2 | Found at home | 3 weeks later | Village 04, Onesa | J2 (J2a read the cards, J2b register and refer) | . | 3 | Made official | 4 weeks later | District Health Center, Onesa | J3 (J3a verify, J3b map and schedule) | . | 4 | Crossing back | 12 months later | Onesa to Taifafeki | J4.0 (a wallet, b share link), J4.1 | . How far a clinician can rely on Somsak’s record, step by step (the journeys walkthrough’s “follow the record” ladder): . | Step | Record state | Held where | FHIR | . | J1 | On paper: two signed DVCs | Khamla’s bag | HC1 QR (HCERT) | . | J2b | Reported, not verified | CHW phone, then sync | Immunization.primarySource false | . | J3a | Verified against the GDHCN trust list | district clinic | Provenance (verifier) | . | J3b | Scheduled: counts toward the national schedule | Onesan national records | schedule coding added, ImmunizationRecommendation, Task | . | J4.0 | Portable: a summary the family can share | Onesan records, link on the phone | IPS Bundle, Consent | . | J4.1 | Shared and audited: viewed abroad, logged at home | Onesan national records | Provenance, AuditEvent | . |   | Process | Where | . | J1 | Issue the newborn’s birth-dose DVCs | Country A | . | J2 | Discover and refer an unregistered infant | Country B | . | J3 | Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic | Country B | . | J4.0 | Issue the family’s records to one phone as VHLs | Country B | . | J4.1 | Read a family member’s records at the point of care abroad | abroad | . Roles, actors and the guides’ actor definitions . Each lane is a role in scenarios/roles.json. Each actor in scenarios/actors/ names the role it plays. Its meta.definedBy gives the ActorDefinitions it is an instance of, and its meta.playsActor gives the smart-trust-tools actor. On the role, the guides’ names appear as otherNames (also known as). | Role (lane) | Actor here | WHO SMART Trust | WHO smart-trust-phw | IHE ITI VHL | smart-trust-tools | . | caregiver | Khamla SENGMANY (J1–J3), Bounmy SENGMANY (J4) | Holder | Holder | VHLHolder | vhl-holder | . | family-phone | the Sengmany family’s shared phone (Bounmy’s) | (Holder’s device) | (Holder’s device: the personal health wallet) | (VHLHolder’s device) | vhl-holder | . | birth-clinic-system | Kesaro Provincial Hospital, Taifafeki | Issuer | Issuer | VHLSharer (HCERT side) | vhl-sharer / hcert-issuing-system | . | issuer-key | XXR’s DSC key (plays Taifafeki) | Trust Network Participant (its PKI) | Trust Network Participant | — | trust-network-participant / hcert-key-holder | . | chw-app | CHW app, Onesa | Receiver (triage read only) | Receiver | VHLReceiver | vhl-receiver / hcert-verifying-system | . | home-clinic-ehr | Lomaru District Health Center EHR | Receiver | Receiver | VHLReceiver | vhl-receiver / hcert-verifying-system | . | gdhcn-trust-anchor | GDHCN DEV (WHO) | Trust Network Anchor | Trust Network Anchor | TrustAnchor | trust-anchor | . | national-portal | Onesa national portal and gateway (XXK) | Issuer; Trust Network Participant | Issuer; Trust Network Participant | VHLSharer | vhl-sharer | . | poc-receiver | Kesaro primary care clinic viewer | Receiver | Receiver | VHLReceiver | vhl-receiver | . | birth-clinic-vaccinator, community-health-worker, home-clinic-provider, poc-provider | Dr Anan, Vilay, Nurse Chanthason, Dr Anan | — (the people operating the systems; no ActorDefinition in either guide) | — | — | — | . smart-trust-phw’s requirements map onto the journeys as follows: . | provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver (Holder) is J2, J3 and J4.1. | receive-a-vhl is J2, J3 and J4.1 too. It names the Issuer as its actor, which looks wrong: OI-01. | publish-, receive-, distribute- and retrieve-pki-material are the trust anchor and the participants in J3. | . User scenarios . Each step names the requirements of smart-trust-tools it exercises, and the FHIR examples of this guide it produces. The stories are in scenarios/stories.json. Each moment ends with its pain point, what enables it, and the policy point it makes, as the journeys walkthrough presents them. J1 — Born abroad (Taifafeki, birth day) . Precondition: the issuer’s DSC is on the trust list. XXR’s document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR’s Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver’s trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Khamla gives birth to Somsak on 2025-10-28 at Kesaro Provincial Hospital, away from home. He has no Taifafeki identity number. Dr Anan gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them with their WHO PreQual product codes. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: . | It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). No identity document is needed (STT-PAY-005). | It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. | It has XXR’s key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. | . Khamla leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the library tests use the WHO guide’s own two signed HC1 strings (QR Code Generation §12), which verify against the live DEV trust list under the same XXR key. Somsak’s DVC payloads are illustrative. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. | Pain point: The baby has no Taifafeki ID number, so his records would normally stay locked inside the Taifafeki hospital’s system. | Enabler: A digitally signed QR card travels with the family — no ID number or database lookup needed. | Policy: Babies born abroad can get a verifiable vaccine record before they have the host country’s civil registration or a national ID — and registering the birth at home still matters. | . J2 — Found at home (Onesa, 3 weeks later) . J2a. On a routine visit to Village 04, Vilay finds a newborn the Onesan system does not know exists. Her phone has had no signal for weeks. Khamla shows the two cards. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, but checks no signature and saves nothing yet. J2b. On the CHW app’s newborn form (structured data capture, TrustDemoHouseholdRegistration) she adds Somsak to the Sengmany household (TrustDemoHousehold), with a temporary id. Bounmy confirms the details as head of household. The app saves the doses read from the cards as reported by the family, not verified (TrustDemoJ2HepBReported, TrustDemoJ2BcgReported: primarySource false). Vilay refers Somsak to the district health center (TrustDemoJ2Referral). Everything stays queued on the phone, for 28 days if need be, and syncs when it next reaches a signal. | Pain point (J2a): Without a check, a forged or mistyped card could quietly become an official record. | Pain point (J2b): Babies born abroad are invisible to the home health system until civil registration catches up — sometimes months later. | Enabler (J2a): The phone reads the card offline, and keeps “what the family told us” clearly separate from “what we have verified”. | Enabler (J2b): An offline form links the baby to his household immediately; it syncs once the phone finds a signal. | Policy (J2a): Keep a clear line between what families report and what has been verified, and don’t grant trust too early. | Policy (J2b): Newborns can be registered at home, offline, before civil registration or a national ID exists. | . J3 — Made official (Lomaru District Health Center, 4 weeks later) . Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR’s DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic’s copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. J3a. Nurse Chanthason opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002), without contacting Taifafeki. Both verify, so it imports them as FHIR Immunizations (TrustDemoJ3HepB, TrustDemoJ3Bcg) with provenance (TrustDemoJ3Verification; STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008), replacing the reported doses of J2. If a DVC fails (a tampered card, say), the EHR names the step and the reason, the doses stay unverified, and the nurse decides by national catch-up policy. J3b. The Taifafeki Hep B product matches nothing on the national schedule. The EHR keeps Taifafeki’s product coding and adds the schedule coding beside it, from the national map (TrustDemoProductToOnesaEpi). For the Hep B product the map has no entry, so Nurse Chanthason makes the clinical call that it is the schedule’s birth dose (TrustDemoJ3Adjudication), and her decision is added to the map for the next clinic. The schedule (TrustDemoOnesaInfantSchedule) then runs: the birth doses count, and pentavalent 1, bOPV 1 and PCV 1 are due at 6 weeks (TrustDemoJ3Recommendation). Khamla leaves with the date (TrustDemoJ3Reminder). Over the year Somsak gets those doses and measles-rubella at 9 months, in Onesa. | Pain point (J3a): Clinicians either distrust foreign paper and re-vaccinate, or trust it blindly. | Pain point (J3b): Countries name and package vaccines differently, so doses get missed or repeated. | Enabler (J3a): Taifafeki’s signing key is on the shared WHO trust list, so any clinic can check it locally. | Enabler (J3b): Taifafeki’s original code is kept and the Onesan code is added alongside; the schedule engine calculates what’s due. | Policy (J3a): Trust is decentralized: an Onesan clinic verifies a Taifafeki signature itself, without contacting Taifafeki. | Policy (J3b): Never overwrite another country’s record: keep the original coding alongside the national one. | . J4.0 — Crossing back: one family, one phone (Onesa, 12 months later) . J4.0a. The family plans a trip to Taifafeki. Bounmy’s phone holds the family wallet, with a profile for each of them. Somsak’s summary (TrustDemoJ4Ips) shows six doses: two from Taifafeki, four from Onesa. Precondition, as in J1: Country B’s DSC, under Country B’s CSCA, is already shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor. That is what lets the clinic in Taifafeki verify the link in J4.1. J4.0b. For Somsak, Bounmy shares his record with a 4-digit passcode he can say aloud, valid for 14 days. The portal records his consent (TrustDemoJ4Consent), then does three things: . | It assembles the IPS and Somsak’s DVCs. | It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). | It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B’s DSC. | . The QR holds only a pointer and a key: the record stays in Onesa. | Pain point (J4.0a): Many families share one smartphone; one-app-per-person designs leave them out. | Pain point (J4.0b): Sending photos or PDFs of records leaks data and can’t be verified by the receiver. | Enabler (J4.0a): A household wallet on one phone, with a separate health summary for each person. | Enabler (J4.0b): A Verifiable Health Link: the QR holds only a locked pointer; the data stays home until the passcode is given. | Policy (J4.0a): Design for shared devices (“One Family, One Phone”) so families with only one phone aren’t left out. | Policy (J4.0b): Data sovereignty: the record stays in Onesa until the family authorizes someone to open it. | . J4.1 — Crossing back: a Taifafeki doctor sees the full history (Kesaro, 12 months later) . Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The clinic viewer’s trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B’s DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The clinic refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Back where it began, Dr Anan sees Somsak at a primary care clinic in Kesaro. Bounmy shows the QR on his phone and says the passcode. The clinic viewer and the Onesan gateway take five steps: . | The viewer verifies the HCERT against Country B’s DSC in its copy of the trust list. | It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). | The Onesan gateway checks the passcode, the expiry and the consent, returns the manifest, and logs the access at home (TrustDemoJ41Access). | The viewer decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007) (TrustDemoJ41Received). | It shows them to Dr Anan: every dose since the birth, viewed, never copied. | . A wrong passcode is refused, and the attempt is still logged in Onesa (TrustDemoJ41WrongPasscode). If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B’s DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The clinic names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Anan treats whatever the family can show as he would a paper record. | Pain point: Without the history, the doctor would repeat vaccines or have to guess. | Enabler: The record is fetched live from Onesa, viewed without being copied, and an access log is sent home. | Policy: Continuity of care across borders: each country keeps its own records, with no international patient registry and no vendor lock-in. What is agreed regionally is the data model and the trust list, not a shared copy of the data. | . Questions for discussion . The journeys walkthrough closes with four policy questions: . | Identity for babies born abroad (J1, J2b): how should national immunization systems handle temporary ids for cross-border infants before civil registration is complete? | Where trust begins (J2a, J3a): why should offline CHW devices store foreign cards as reported, not verified, rather than verify them in the field? | Matching vaccines across countries (J3b): when a monovalent vaccine is given abroad but the home schedule uses a combination (pentavalent), how should schedule rules count the doses still due? | Cross-border access and audit (J4.0b, J4.1): what agreements do countries need so that a clinician viewing a record abroad triggers an audit entry in the patient’s home country? | . Dr. Anan (Taifafeki clinician · birth & follow-up, Taifafeki) . Persona: a Taifafeki clinician in Kesaro who gives Somsak’s Hep B and BCG birth doses and prints the two signed DVCs (J1), and who sees him again a year later at a primary care clinic, reading his record through the VHL (J4.1). Fictional. | Goal: Give a non-Taifafeki baby proper care, at birth and when he returns. | Needs: A way to issue records that travel with the family; A child’s full history at the point of care; Confidence the data is authentic | Frustrations: No national ID to attach records to; Records from abroad he cannot read or verify | . Creates Somsak’s passcode-protected VHL (J4.0) and says the passcode aloud at the clinic (J4.1). Fictional. | Goal: Keep the whole family’s health records in one place he controls. | Needs: One app for three people on one phone; Share records abroad without paperwork; Decide who sees what, and for how long | Frustrations: Carrying folders of documents across the border; Not knowing who has seen his child’s data | . Fictional. | Goal: Trust foreign records enough to avoid repeating or missing vaccines. | Needs: A reliable yes/no on whether a card is genuine; Foreign vaccines translated to the Onesan schedule; Automatic calculation of what is due next | Frustrations: Unfamiliar product names from other countries; Choosing between re-vaccinating and trusting paper blindly | . Fictional. | Goal: Have Somsak’s care recognized at home, without starting over. | Needs: Proof of the vaccines her baby got abroad; Clear guidance on when to come back; Not to be penalized for giving birth across the border | Frustrations: Paper cards are easy to lose; Extra trips to the clinic; The family’s records live on her husband’s phone | . Somsak (Baby · the record follows him, Onesa) . The subject of every journey: an Onesan baby boy born 2025-10-28 at Kesaro Provincial Hospital, Taifafeki (Country A), while his family lives in Onesa (Country B). Has no Taifafeki identity number; registered in Onesa with a temporary id by the CHW (J2). Holds no device and acts through his parents. The story is the VaxLink workshop walkthrough’s (fredhersch/vaxlink). Fictional. | Goal: Get every vaccine he needs, once, wherever he is. | Needs: His birth doses to count at home; No repeated or missed vaccines; His history to be there when a doctor needs it | Frustrations: Born where he has no national ID; Invisible to the home system until someone registers him | . Vilay (Community health worker · Village 04, Onesa) . Persona for J2: the community health worker of catchment Village 04 in Onesa (Country B). Works offline for weeks at a time on an Android phone (OHS app, community configuration) and syncs when she reaches the health center. Can register a child and refer, but cannot decide whether a foreign record is genuine. Fictional. | Goal: Make sure no newborn in her village is missed, even with no signal. | Needs: Tools that work offline for weeks; A fast way to capture foreign cards; A clear next step to hand the family | Frustrations: Can’t confirm whether a foreign card is genuine; Paperwork that duplicates what the clinic does | . 513f2e9ee8ce.title: Plan
513f2e9ee8ce.content: . Each step is one pull request, merged when CI is green. Decisions that are the owner’s are asked before the step that needs them and recorded in memory/. Decisions so far (2026-10-23) . | Decision | Choice | Record | . | Library consumption | Build the JVM jars in CI from a pinned smart-trust-tools commit | memory/dir-library-consumption.md | . | Harness | Full cat-harness downstream of smart-trust-tools | memory/dir-downstream.md | . | Home country (J2–J4) | A fictional GDHCN DEV participant; J1’s issuer stays XXR | memory/dir-journeys-demo.md | . | OHS base for the app | Option B, staged; Rust/wasm for the web meanwhile (proposals/app-platform.md) | memory/dir-app-platform.md | . | IG identity | smart.who.int.trust-demo, http://smart.who.int/trust-demo | memory/dir-ig-identity.md | . Steps . 1. Plan and skeleton (this PR) . README (including the smart-trust-phw upstream note), AGENTS.md, this plan, the app-platform proposal, owner directives in memory/, the dependency register, and a CI job that checks every GitHub Action is pinned by commit SHA and every JSON file parses. 2. Journeys as cat-harness content . | (done) smart-trust-demo.json declaration and index.config.json pinning the harness layers smart-trust-tools pins (fhir-harness and below) plus smart-trust-tools itself, so req: ids resolve; index.lock.json. | scenarios/: the actors (reusing smart-trust-tools’ VHL Holder, Sharer, Receiver, Trust Network Participant), the roles that play lanes, and the personas: the mother and newborn (J1’s IG example), the J1 clinic nurse, the CHW (J2), the home clinic provider (J3), the national portal and the border/clinic receiver abroad (J4). | processes/content/: one BPMN per journey (done in step 2a; checklists and the harness mount in 2b) (J1 issuance, J2 CHW discovery and referral, J3 verification, import and schedule, J4.0 VHL issuance to a shared phone, J4.1 VHL fetch at the point of care), lanes naming roles, tasks naming smart-trust-tools skills; checklists generated. | User scenarios: one per journey, each step tracing to req: nodes (e.g. J2 → STT-VER-011, J3 → STT-VER-001…, J4 → the VHL requirements). | Beans for gaps found on the way (in this repository, or tagged upstream for smart-trust-tools, smart-trust or smart-trust-phw). | . 2c. L2 DAK and L3 FHIR IG . The journeys as a WHO SMART Guidelines DAK and FHIR IG, shaped as litlfred/smart-immunizations (sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini, the DAK in index.config.json (contentTypes.dak), input/). The L2 content is generated from the harness sources by tools/ig-gen/ig_gen.py: roles become ActorDefinitions, the BPMN is copied to input/business-processes/, stories and scenarios become pages. CI checks the generated files are current and that SUSHI builds with no errors. Then: publish the IG on gh-pages and add example resources per journey (bean IG-01). 3. The HCERT library at a pinned commit . lib/hcert/: a script and Gradle wiring that checks out smart-trust-tools at a pinned SHA, builds hcert-api and hcert-core (JVM) with that repository’s own Gradle and verification-metadata.xml, and copies the jars to lib/hcert/build/libs/, failing if a jar’s sha256 differs from the one recorded in lib/hcert/hcert.lock.json (the build is reproducible). The app and the Android tests depend on those files. Bumping the library is the commit in the lock plus build.py --update. 4. Android emulator test of the library (STT-GEN-004) . (In progress: android-test/ and .github/workflows/android.yml. The Gradle verification metadata is written on GitHub’s runner, since this session cannot reach Google Maven.) . android-test/: an Android library module whose instrumented tests run on an emulator in CI (Android API levels to be chosen: one current, one old enough to matter for clinics, e.g. 26 and 35): . | verify the IG’s §12 example against XXR’s DSC DID document (the DEV trust list), on Android’s platform providers; | readUnverified of the same QR (J2); | issue with an Android Keystore key (prepare → Keystore sign → finish) and verify it, ES256, and PS256 where the platform offers it; | VHL: build and read a vhlink:/, decrypt the JWE fixture. | . Results are reported back to smart-trust-tools as evidence for STT-GEN-004 (and as beans there for anything Android refuses, e.g. algorithm names). Google Maven artifacts (AGP, AndroidX test) are pinned with sha256 like every other. The emulator job uses a pinned action by SHA and caches no unverified artifacts. 5. The app . (Started: app/, J2’s offline read, and J3’s verification and import of the guide’s DVCs on Android, workflow app.yml. A verified DVC becomes a FHIR R4 Immunization with its Provenance (dev.ohs.fhir:fhir-model-r4); an unverified one is not imported. Next: J3’s schedule, then J1 issuance.) . An emulator UI test drives the four journeys end to end. 6. Web and publication . The web target (once hcert-core runs in a browser, or via the Rust/wasm library meanwhile), and the gh-pages site (agent-published): the journeys, BPMN viewers, personas and the test evidence. Steps 4–5 need it locally to write the verification metadata; the owner can allow it in the environment’s network settings. | Browser build of hcert-core (for the web target): to be raised in smart-trust-tools. | Android algorithm names: hcert-core’s JVM code asks for RSASSA-PSS, which Android’s providers may not offer under that name; step 4 will show. | . 225179d472a9.title: App Platform Proposal
225179d472a9.content: . Status: decided 2026-10-23: option B, staged, with the Rust/wasm library for the web meanwhile (memory/dir-app-platform.md). Researched 2026-10-23. Question: on what should the J1–J4 app be built, so that it runs the Kotlin HCERT library on Android (and, ideally, the web) on the most recent, most Kotlin-native Open Health Stack? . 1. What Open Health Stack is today . Open Health Stack (OHS) began as a Google-led set of components and is now the OHS Software Foundation, a community project under the Linux Foundation, which WHO joined in July 2026. Its code lives in github.com/ohs-foundation (28 repositories). There are two generations of the client libraries: . | Generation | Libraries | Platforms | Distribution | State | . | android-fhir (first) | com.google.android.fhir:engine, data-capture (SDC), workflow, knowledge | Android only | Google Maven | “Maintenance”; last commit Feb–Mar 2026. Workflow runs CQL (HAPI-based, heavy). | . | Kotlin Multiplatform (current) | dev.ohs.fhir:fhir-model-r4 1.0.0-rc03, fhir-path-r4, fhir-engine 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-data-capture 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-workflow 2.0.0-alpha01; dev.ohs.player:client 1.0.0-alpha03 | Android, desktop JVM, iOS, web (wasmJs, and JS for some) | Maven Central | Active (commits this week); alpha APIs. Workflow does PlanDefinition/$apply; CQL is “still to come”. | . On top of the KMP generation sits the OHS Player, described by the foundation as a cross-stack reference toolkit, “reference, not product”: . | player-reference: the client, a GitHub template app in Compose Multiplatform (Android, iOS, desktop, web from one tree). Screens are driven by configuration (SQL-on-FHIR ViewDefinitions compiled at build time), data entry by SDC questionnaires. It opens on an OIDC login and blocks on a first sync with a FHIR server; there is no bundled-data mode. | player-client: the library behind it (configuration-driven FHIR views), usable on its own. | ohs-player-reference-web-portal: a TypeScript admin portal for workforce hierarchies (users, access). Not a clinical web app; not relevant to J1–J4. | ohs-player-reference-backend, -infrastructure: backend and deployment (FHIR gateway, data pipes). | player-reference-examples: variants of the reference app (empty today). A natural place to offer the journeys upstream later — an OHS Foundation repository, so only by proposal, never from here. | . The most recent and most Kotlin-native choice is therefore the KMP generation, with or without the Player template. 2. Constraints every option must meet . | The Android emulator test of the HCERT library (STT-GEN-004) must run in CI on an Android runtime, platform crypto included. This is independent of the app: it is a small Android test module that depends only on the HCERT jar (plan step 4). It can land before the app decision. | Offline and serverless demo. J2 is offline by definition, and CI cannot stand up an OIDC provider and FHIR server for an emulator run cheaply. The app needs a bundled-data mode. | Supply chain. Every artifact pinned with sha256, releases ≥ 14 days old, no install scripts. Fewer dependencies is better. | The HCERT library comes from a pinned smart-trust-tools commit as a JVM jar (owner’s choice). On Android the JVM jar works as is. On the web it does not yet: hcert-core’s Kotlin/JS target uses node:crypto and node:zlib, so it runs on Node, not in a browser, and there is no wasmJs target. Any web front end needs either a browser target in hcert-core (WebCrypto, CompressionStream), a library change in smart-trust-tools, or the Rust/wasm library, which already runs in the browser with WebCrypto keys. | . 3. Options . Option A — Fork the OHS Player reference app . Create the app from the player-reference template; add an offline demo mode (bundled FHIR bundle, no login), the J1–J4 screens and the HCERT calls. | Pros | Cons | . | It is the OHS Player: the most visibly “OHS” outcome, and the closest to what OHS implementers will start from. | Requires an OIDC provider and a FHIR server to start; the offline mode is ours to write and to keep merging against a template that moves weekly. | . | Android, iOS, desktop and web from one tree; configuration-driven screens; SDC questionnaires for registration (J2) and import (J3) come wired. | ~57 libraries and 8 plugins in its catalogue (Koin, Ktor CIO/Darwin, Kermit, ksafe, kotlinpoet, BigNum, Compose adaptive …), several alpha, plus their transitive graph: the largest pinning and verification burden of all options. | . | Upstreamable: journeys could later become a variant in player-reference-examples. | Kotlin 2.3 / AGP 8.11 / JDK 21; its build-logic and code generation (ig-codegen) are ours to audit. | . |   | Much of the template (auth, sync, workforce registers) is unrelated to the journeys and is noise in a demonstrator. | . Option B — Own lean Compose Multiplatform app on the OHS KMP libraries (recommended) . A small Compose Multiplatform app (Android first, web target alongside) written for the four journeys, using the same foundational libraries the Player uses — fhir-model-r4, fhir-engine (on-device store), fhir-data-capture (SDC questionnaires for J2 registration and J3 import), fhir-workflow (PlanDefinition/$apply for the J3 schedule) — and, optionally, dev.ohs.player:client for configuration-driven views. | Pros | Cons | . | Same current OHS libraries as the Player, so it demonstrates the stack the OHS Foundation is building towards, without the template’s auth/sync/DI layer. | Not the Player app itself; screens are ours. | . | Offline and serverless from the start; the emulator CI job can drive the journeys. | The KMP libraries are alpha: API breaks between alphas are ours to absorb. | . | Dependency set is roughly the libraries’ own graph (Compose MP, Ktor client, Room3/SQLite, kotlinx) — still sizeable, but every addition is chosen and listed in docs/dependencies.md. | fhir-workflow has no CQL yet: the J3 schedule rules must be expressed as PlanDefinition applicability conditions in FHIRPath (enough for a birth-dose schedule; WHO SMART immunization CQL would wait). | . | Shapes the code so the journey screens can later be offered to player-reference-examples as a Player variant. |   | . Option C — Android only, on android-fhir (first generation) . A plain Android app on com.google.android.fhir Engine + SDC (+ Workflow). | Pros | Cons | . | Mature, production-proven (OpenSRP, EmCare); most documentation and examples. | In maintenance; not where OHS is going; Android only (no web). | . | Workflow library runs CQL today (WHO SMART Guidelines content). | Workflow pulls HAPI FHIR + CQL engine: a very large, JVM-heavy dependency graph. | . |   | Google Maven artifacts; the session’s network policy currently blocks dl.google.com (needed for this and for AGP/AndroidX in every option). | . Option D — Web first, no Android app . A static page on gh-pages running J1–J4 in the browser with the Rust/wasm library (or a future browser build of hcert-core), plus only the Android test module for STT-GEN-004. | Pros | Cons | . | Smallest: almost no dependencies; easiest to show anyone with a link. | Not OHS; does not show the Kotlin library inside an OHS app, which is the stated goal. | . | The Rust/wasm library already runs in the browser. | The Kotlin library on Android is exercised only by tests, not by a journey. | . 4. Recommendation . Option B, staged: . | Android test module for STT-GEN-004 first (independent of this choice). | The B app, Android target, offline, J1–J4, on dev.ohs.fhir engine + data capture + workflow. | The web target of the same app once hcert-core has a browser target (to be requested in smart-trust-tools) — or, in the meantime, the journeys’ QR steps on the web through the Rust/wasm library. | Later, propose the journeys to the OHS Foundation as a player-reference-examples variant (owner’s call; never pushed from here). | . If being the OHS Player matters more than dependency count and an offline demo, choose A: the plan is the same, with step 2 starting from the template and adding the offline mode first. 5. What any option needs from the environment . | dl.google.com (Google Maven: AGP, AndroidX, the Android SDK) is blocked by this session’s network policy. It is needed to write the Gradle verification metadata for any Android build. GitHub’s runners can reach it, so CI is unaffected; local builds here are. | . dec3fb9c6787.title: User Scenarios
dec3fb9c6787.content: . User stories . Each story traces to the smart-trust-tools requirements that serve it (scenarios/story-requirements.json); where the HCERT library does not serve a story, the note says what does. | Role | I want to | So that | Requirements | . | Caregiver | Have my son’s birth doses from abroad recognised at home | his care does not start over and nothing is repeated | STT-VER-001, STT-VER-009, STT-TRU-002 | . | Caregiver | Show each family member’s records abroad from our one shared phone, with a passcode I can say aloud | a doctor abroad can treat us without paper or an app | STD-ACC-001, STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002, STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007 | . | Caregiver | Decide who sees my child’s record, and for how long | the record stays at home and I know who has looked | STD-ACC-001, STT-VHL-009, STT-VHL-008 | . | Birth clinic vaccinator | Print a signed record of each birth dose the family can carry anywhere |   | STT-PAY-001, STT-PAY-003, STT-ISS-004, STT-COS-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001 | . | Community health worker | Read a foreign vaccination QR offline and register the child with it | the clinic sees what was given before the family arrives | STT-VER-011, STT-B45-002, STT-CBR-003 | . | Community health worker | Refer a child whose foreign record needs checking | verification is done by someone who can | STT-VER-011 | . | Community health worker | Register a newborn into the household offline, before civil registration | no newborn in my village is missed, even with no signal | STT-PAY-005 | . | Home clinic provider | Know whether a foreign certificate is genuine, and why not when it is not |   | STT-VER-001, STT-VER-002, STT-VER-008, STT-TRU-001 | . | Home clinic provider | See which doses are due once the foreign doses are imported | I give only what is missing | STD-SCH-001 | . | Home clinic provider | Keep the foreign vaccine code and add our schedule code beside it, deciding myself when there is no match | the other country’s record is never overwritten and the next nurse need not decide again | STD-SEM-001 | . | Point-of-care provider | Read a visiting child’s summary and vaccinations from a QR the parent shows | without installing anything or calling another country | STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-007, STT-VHL-008 | . | Point-of-care provider | Know the record I read abroad came from the child’s home country and was not altered | I can rely on it as I would on my own clinic’s record | STT-VER-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-KID-002 | . User scenarios . Each step names the requirements of smart-trust-tools it exercises, and the FHIR examples of this guide it produces. The stories are in scenarios/stories.json. Each moment ends with its pain point, what enables it, and the policy point it makes, as the journeys walkthrough presents them. J1 — Born abroad (Taifafeki, birth day) . Precondition: the issuer’s DSC is on the trust list. XXR’s document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR’s Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver’s trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Khamla gives birth to Somsak on 2025-10-28 at Kesaro Provincial Hospital, away from home. He has no Taifafeki identity number. Dr Anan gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them with their WHO PreQual product codes. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: . | It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). No identity document is needed (STT-PAY-005). | It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. | It has XXR’s key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. | . Khamla leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the library tests use the WHO guide’s own two signed HC1 strings (QR Code Generation §12), which verify against the live DEV trust list under the same XXR key. Somsak’s DVC payloads are illustrative. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. | Pain point: The baby has no Taifafeki ID number, so his records would normally stay locked inside the Taifafeki hospital’s system. | Enabler: A digitally signed QR card travels with the family — no ID number or database lookup needed. | Policy: Babies born abroad can get a verifiable vaccine record before they have the host country’s civil registration or a national ID — and registering the birth at home still matters. | . J2 — Found at home (Onesa, 3 weeks later) . J2a. On a routine visit to Village 04, Vilay finds a newborn the Onesan system does not know exists. Her phone has had no signal for weeks. Khamla shows the two cards. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, but checks no signature and saves nothing yet. J2b. On the CHW app’s newborn form (structured data capture, TrustDemoHouseholdRegistration) she adds Somsak to the Sengmany household (TrustDemoHousehold), with a temporary id. Bounmy confirms the details as head of household. The app saves the doses read from the cards as reported by the family, not verified (TrustDemoJ2HepBReported, TrustDemoJ2BcgReported: primarySource false). Vilay refers Somsak to the district health center (TrustDemoJ2Referral). Everything stays queued on the phone, for 28 days if need be, and syncs when it next reaches a signal. | Pain point (J2a): Without a check, a forged or mistyped card could quietly become an official record. | Pain point (J2b): Babies born abroad are invisible to the home health system until civil registration catches up — sometimes months later. | Enabler (J2a): The phone reads the card offline, and keeps “what the family told us” clearly separate from “what we have verified”. | Enabler (J2b): An offline form links the baby to his household immediately; it syncs once the phone finds a signal. | Policy (J2a): Keep a clear line between what families report and what has been verified, and don’t grant trust too early. | Policy (J2b): Newborns can be registered at home, offline, before civil registration or a national ID exists. | . J3 — Made official (Lomaru District Health Center, 4 weeks later) . Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR’s DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic’s copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. J3a. Nurse Chanthason opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002), without contacting Taifafeki. Both verify, so it imports them as FHIR Immunizations (TrustDemoJ3HepB, TrustDemoJ3Bcg) with provenance (TrustDemoJ3Verification; STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008), replacing the reported doses of J2. If a DVC fails (a tampered card, say), the EHR names the step and the reason, the doses stay unverified, and the nurse decides by national catch-up policy. J3b. The Taifafeki Hep B product matches nothing on the national schedule. The EHR keeps Taifafeki’s product coding and adds the schedule coding beside it, from the national map (TrustDemoProductToOnesaEpi). For the Hep B product the map has no entry, so Nurse Chanthason makes the clinical call that it is the schedule’s birth dose (TrustDemoJ3Adjudication), and her decision is added to the map for the next clinic. The schedule (TrustDemoOnesaInfantSchedule) then runs: the birth doses count, and pentavalent 1, bOPV 1 and PCV 1 are due at 6 weeks (TrustDemoJ3Recommendation). Khamla leaves with the date (TrustDemoJ3Reminder). Over the year Somsak gets those doses and measles-rubella at 9 months, in Onesa. | Pain point (J3a): Clinicians either distrust foreign paper and re-vaccinate, or trust it blindly. | Pain point (J3b): Countries name and package vaccines differently, so doses get missed or repeated. | Enabler (J3a): Taifafeki’s signing key is on the shared WHO trust list, so any clinic can check it locally. | Enabler (J3b): Taifafeki’s original code is kept and the Onesan code is added alongside; the schedule engine calculates what’s due. | Policy (J3a): Trust is decentralized: an Onesan clinic verifies a Taifafeki signature itself, without contacting Taifafeki. | Policy (J3b): Never overwrite another country’s record: keep the original coding alongside the national one. | . J4.0 — Crossing back: one family, one phone (Onesa, 12 months later) . J4.0a. The family plans a trip to Taifafeki. Bounmy’s phone holds the family wallet, with a profile for each of them. Somsak’s summary (TrustDemoJ4Ips) shows six doses: two from Taifafeki, four from Onesa. Precondition, as in J1: Country B’s DSC, under Country B’s CSCA, is already shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor. That is what lets the clinic in Taifafeki verify the link in J4.1. J4.0b. For Somsak, Bounmy shares his record with a 4-digit passcode he can say aloud, valid for 14 days. The portal records his consent (TrustDemoJ4Consent), then does three things: . | It assembles the IPS and Somsak’s DVCs. | It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). | It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B’s DSC. | . The QR holds only a pointer and a key: the record stays in Onesa. | Pain point (J4.0a): Many families share one smartphone; one-app-per-person designs leave them out. | Pain point (J4.0b): Sending photos or PDFs of records leaks data and can’t be verified by the receiver. | Enabler (J4.0a): A household wallet on one phone, with a separate health summary for each person. | Enabler (J4.0b): A Verifiable Health Link: the QR holds only a locked pointer; the data stays home until the passcode is given. | Policy (J4.0a): Design for shared devices (“One Family, One Phone”) so families with only one phone aren’t left out. | Policy (J4.0b): Data sovereignty: the record stays in Onesa until the family authorizes someone to open it. | . J4.1 — Crossing back: a Taifafeki doctor sees the full history (Kesaro, 12 months later) . Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The clinic viewer’s trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B’s DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The clinic refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Back where it began, Dr Anan sees Somsak at a primary care clinic in Kesaro. Bounmy shows the QR on his phone and says the passcode. The clinic viewer and the Onesan gateway take five steps: . | The viewer verifies the HCERT against Country B’s DSC in its copy of the trust list. | It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). | The Onesan gateway checks the passcode, the expiry and the consent, returns the manifest, and logs the access at home (TrustDemoJ41Access). | The viewer decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007) (TrustDemoJ41Received). | It shows them to Dr Anan: every dose since the birth, viewed, never copied. | . A wrong passcode is refused, and the attempt is still logged in Onesa (TrustDemoJ41WrongPasscode). If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B’s DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The clinic names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Anan treats whatever the family can show as he would a paper record. | Pain point: Without the history, the doctor would repeat vaccines or have to guess. | Enabler: The record is fetched live from Onesa, viewed without being copied, and an access log is sent home. | Policy: Continuity of care across borders: each country keeps its own records, with no international patient registry and no vendor lock-in. What is agreed regionally is the data model and the trust list, not a shared copy of the data. | . Edit this page on GitHub .

e4fbe9ce6c41.content: . Filed as smart-trust-phw#18; fix offered as smart-trust-phw#19. Title: Requirement receive-a-vhl names the Issuer as its actor; it should be the Receiver . In input/fsh/requirements/requirements.fsh, the Requirements instance receive-a-vhl (“Receive VHL or VDHC”) reads: . * description = "Is able to receive a VHL authorization mechanism or a VDHC from a Holder" * actor[+] = Canonical(Issuer) . The capability described, receiving a VHL or VDHC from a Holder, is the Receiver’s (ActorDefinition/Receiver: “Receiver (system) of Verifiable Health Certificate or Verifiable Health Link”). Its counterpart provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver names the Holder. Proposed fix: . -* actor[+] = Canonical(Issuer) +* actor[+] = Canonical(Receiver) . The same change is applied in litlfred/smart-trust-phw (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-phw/pull/1) and can be offered as a pull request here. Found while mapping the user journeys of litlfred/smart-trust-demo (a CHW app, a clinic EHR and a hospital system abroad each receive a VDHC or VHL from the Holder) to the guide’s actors.
